title: Salisbury steak
subtitle: American seasoned beef patties in mushroom-onion gravy
excerpt: Oval seasoned beef patties pan-fried and then simmered in a rich mushroom-and-onion brown gravy. American diner comfort food at its best, served with mashed potato.
sourceNotes: Salisbury steak was named after Dr James Salisbury (1823 to 1905), an American physician who promoted a meat-heavy diet. The dish became a staple of American diner cooking and TV dinner culture, appearing in Joy of Cooking and in numerous American home cooking texts throughout the twentieth century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The patties can be shaped and refrigerated up to a day ahead.

content.text: Salisbury steak is a hamburger patty given an oval shape and drowned in mushroom-onion gravy. It is American diner food from the 1950s and it is extremely good. The patties cook in the gravy for part of the time. They absorb the sauce and stay moist while the gravy thickens around them.
Combine all the patty ingredients in a bowl and mix until just combined. Divide into 4 portions and shape each into an oval about 2 cm thick.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Brown the patties for 3 minutes per side until a crust forms. Remove from the pan and set aside. They do not need to be cooked through at this stage.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter to the pan. Cook the onion for 8 minutes until softened and starting to turn golden. Add the mushrooms and cook for 5 minutes. Add the flour and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the stock and Worcestershire sauce, stirring constantly. Bring to a simmer.
Return the patties to the pan and spoon the gravy over them. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes until the patties are cooked through and the gravy has thickened. Serve with mashed potato.

items.cause: Not enough flour, or not simmered long enough
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for another 5 minutes. Mix 1 teaspoon of cornflour with a little cold water and stir into the gravy if needed.

content.text: Salisbury steak became a fixture of American diner menus from the early twentieth century. Its peak cultural moment was the Swanson TV dinner era of the 1950s and 1960s. The frozen version in the foil tray was one of America's best-selling TV dinners. The homemade version, with proper mushroom gravy, is completely different.
